items.title: Jay McShann interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: He was to perform later that night with former bandmates Jimmy Witherspoon and Claude “Fiddler” Williams.

ctx.x: Pianist and band leader Jay McShann was born in Oklahoma in 1916. He can speak first-hand about the hot bed of jazz that was Kansas City in the 1930s. As a contemporary of Count Basie, Jay was in on the formative years of big band swing and his blues based piano style has fortunately been recorded consistently since the late 30s. He was instrumental in producing hit records for blues vocalists Walter Brown and Jimmy Witherspoon and will hold a place in jazz history as Charlie Parker’s first serious employer. Jay…
Jay was interviewed by Monk Rowe at the Sarasota Jazz Festival on April 12, 1996. He was to perform later that night with former bandmates Jimmy Witherspoon and Claude “Fiddler” Williams.

We are filming today for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive and it’s a great honor to have Jay McShann with us today, piano player and band leader and interesting figure. Thanks so much for joining us.

items.title: Claude Williams interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 4, 1995
items.q: I was with Jay McShann. We played a blues festival in Chicago.

ctx.x: Tell us about working with Buddy Tate.

Oh, well I knew Buddy from Texas or wherever he was from. And I ran into him because I was down there with a band, a territory band down there by name of Alphonso Trent. He was the first black band that played in the Adolphus Hotel in Dallas. And he was pretty well known all over Texas, Alphonso, so Buddy had worked with Alphonso around there in Texas. Something happened and the band finally broke up. And then T. Holder was down there with a different group. And he had picked up Buddy. And we played together in…

but all musicians who are supposed to be from 65 up, you know. They call it “elder statesmen.” So I had Buddy to come over, and went over in New York, and his picture is on one thing. We made him blow a few tunes and I made him play on one tune on the tape, but he’s still weak you know, kind of sick. We had Buddy one night, it must have been about five or six years ago, I was with Jay McShann. We played a blues festival in Chicago.
